econ_conditions: Hyperinflation 1923 destroyed savings; Great Depression -30% GDP 1929–32; mass unemployment 30% by 1932; reparations debt structurally crippling state finances
social: WWI trauma + stab-in-the-back myth; extreme political polarisation — street violence normalised; middle class economically annihilated turned to extremes; antisemitic scapegoating filling explanatory vacuum
institutional: Proportional representation producing ungovernable coalitions; Article 48 emergency powers used 109 times by 1932; presidential system enabling chancellor bypass of parliament; judiciary sympathetic to right-wing violence
political: NSDAP 2.6% (1928) → 37.4% (1932) in 4 years; elite conservatives miscalculated they could control Hitler; SA street violence making normal politics impossible; Communist threat used to justify emergency measures
external: Versailles humiliation as perpetual mobilising grievance; US credit withdrawal post-1929 crashed economy; French and British appeasement enabling boldness
unique_aspects: Speed of collapse — functioning republic to dictatorship in 63 days after Hitler's appointment. Elite miscalculation (von Papen believing Hitler was controllable) is the single most studied error in democratic collapse literature. No other case moves this fast.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Bundesarchiv; Institut für Zeitgeschichte München; Reichstag election records

econ_conditions: Agrarian economy with extreme inequality; land reform stalled by landlord resistance; industrial north vs agrarian south structural divide; foreign capital flight after 1931 Republic declaration
social: Church vs secular deep cultural fracture; regional nationalist movements (Catalonia, Basque); extreme class polarisation — landless peasants vs latifundistas; political assassinations normalising violence before war
institutional: Young republic with weak legitimacy on all sides; military with tradition of pronunciamiento; Church as parallel institutional power hostile to Republic; no consensus on constitutional rules between factions
political: Left-right polarisation leaving no centre ground; Popular Front electoral win triggering military response; anarchist/socialist/communist left unable to unify; Franco coup supported by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy
external: Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy military support to Franco; Soviet Union support to Republic creating ideological dependency; non-intervention by France and Britain despite treaty obligations
unique_aspects: Only case producing full civil war rather than coup or electoral takeover. Intensity of pre-existing social fracture lines (class, religion, region) made negotiated resolution impossible. Three separate left factions fighting each other simultaneously.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Archivo General de la Guerra Civil Española; Preston biography documentation

econ_conditions: Allende copper nationalisation threatening US corporate interests; hyperinflation engineered partly by CIA economic destabilisation; truckers strike (externally funded) paralyzing supply chains; black market and hoarding creating artificial scarcity
social: Middle class radicalised by economic chaos and scarcity; class polarisation but less ethnic/religious than other cases; polarised media — no neutral information environment; women's march of empty pots as middle class opposition symbol
institutional: Military with strong professional tradition — coup was not inevitable; Supreme Court and Congress declaring Allende's actions unconstitutional; Christian Democratic Party withdrawing support enabling coup justification; constitution ambiguous on civilian control limits
political: Allende won with only 36% — never majority mandate; opposition gained congressional majority 1973 midterms; US actively funding opposition parties and destabilisation; coup planned and executed within 3 years of electoral win
external: CIA Operation FUBELT — active destabilisation programme; ITT Corporation lobbying Nixon for intervention; Nixon economic blockade cutting international credit; Kissinger: I don't see why we need to stand by and watch Chile go communist
unique_aspects: Fastest collapse from functioning democracy in the library — 3 years. External interference was decisive, not just contributory. Without CIA destabilisation the economic crisis may have been manageable. Two-level game: domestic polarisation plus external intervention.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; CONADEP equivalent (Rettig Report); US National Security Archive declassified CIA documents

econ_conditions: Oil wealth creating parallel economy bypassing traditional bazaar; rapid modernisation creating displaced traditional middle class; inequality between oil-connected elite and rural/religious poor; inflation from oil boom spending destabilising living costs
social: Secularisation programme alienating religious establishment; SAVAK political repression eliminating moderate opposition; bazaari merchant class alienated by economic modernisation; students and clergy forming unlikely revolutionary coalition
institutional: Shah's personal rule had hollowed all institutions; military loyalty to person not state — collapsed with Shah's departure; no legitimate opposition party to channel dissent; SAVAK created fear but also demonstrated regime fragility
political: Khomeini providing ideological framework from exile in Paris; Carter human rights pressure forcing Shah to ease repression — destabilising; mass strikes in oil sector economically decisive; no negotiated transition possible — complete revolutionary replacement
external: Carter human rights policy reducing US support for Shah; Khomeini exile in France gave him Western media platform; Iraq and regional neighbours watching for opportunity
unique_aspects: Only case producing theocratic replacement rather than military or electoral outcome. Revolution consumed its moderate allies once clerical structure consolidated. Mosque network as parallel organisational infrastructure — only meeting spaces SAVAK couldn't fully monitor.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; National Security Archive Iran; Abrahamian academic documentation

econ_conditions: Post-WWI economic dislocation and unemployment; fear of socialist revolution after factory occupations 1920; inflation and debt from war financing; northern industrial elite funding Fascist squads as strike-breakers
social: Returning WWI veterans feeling betrayed by mutilated victory; middle class fear of socialist redistribution; nationalist frustration at Versailles outcomes; squadrismo normalising political violence in rural areas
institutional: Liberal state deliberately weakened by Giolittian trasformismo; King Victor Emmanuel III refused to declare martial law against March on Rome; Acerbo Law 1923 converting plurality into supermajority; Matteotti murder 1924 — opposition boycott played into Mussolini's hands
political: March on Rome 1922 — bluff that worked because elites capitulated; gradual legal consolidation rather than immediate dictatorship; opposition parties banned incrementally 1925–1928; press censorship introduced step by step not all at once
external: Mussolini presented as bulwark against Bolshevism — Western acceptance; Lateran Treaty with Vatican neutralising Catholic opposition; no significant foreign pressure against consolidation
unique_aspects: Slowest consolidation in library — 6 years from power to full dictatorship. Each step legalised before the next taken. Boiling frog pattern: no single moment where opposition could say this is the line. Elite miscalculation that Mussolini was controllable mirrors Weimar exactly.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Archivio Centrale dello Stato; De Felice Mussolini biography

econ_conditions: Post-WWII commodity export boom funding social spending; nationalisation of railways and utilities building state patronage; Peronist wage increases buying labour movement loyalty; import substitution industrialisation creating protected industries
social: Descamisados as political base; Eva Perón as social mobility symbol for working class; university autonomy attacked — intellectuals alienated; traditional elite and Church eventually turning against regime
institutional: Supreme Court impeached and replaced 1947; constitution rewritten 1949 allowing re-election; Peronist party controlling trade unions as transmission belt; opposition press closed or transferred to regime allies
political: Electoral legitimacy maintained throughout — never banned elections; personalismo — party identity fused with leader identity; military coup 1955 ending regime; Eva's death 1952 removing key legitimising figure
external: Cold War context — US ambivalent given anti-communist posture; Perón's Third Position ideology creating strategic ambiguity; British interests threatened by nationalisations
unique_aspects: First fully developed populist playbook — later replicated by Chávez, Erdoğan, Orbán almost exactly. Electoral legitimacy never abandoned; institutions transformed from within. Evita factor: personalisation via charismatic second figure unique and proved critical to popular legitimacy.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; AGN Argentina; Luna biography; Latinobarómetro historical

econ_conditions: Oil nationalisation 1938 as nationalist founding myth; miracle economy 1940–70: 6% annual growth; 1982 debt crisis beginning PRI legitimacy erosion; NAFTA 1994 triggering Zapatista uprising — contradictions made visible
social: Mestizo national identity construction absorbing regional identities; corporatist structure: unions, peasants, popular sector all in PRI; Tlatelolco massacre 1968 — student movement crushed; gradual civil society emergence 1980s challenging corporatism
institutional: Perfect dictatorship (Vargas Llosa phrase); no re-election rule for president giving regularised elite circulation; electoral fraud systematic but graduated — allow some opposition wins; IFE electoral commission gradually gaining independence 1990s
political: 65-year single party rule without formal dictatorship declaration; sexenio rhythm: 6-year cycles providing predictability; co-optation before repression as primary control mechanism; 1988 election stolen from Cárdenas — legitimacy crisis beginning
external: US acceptance as stable anti-communist neighbour; NAFTA integration creating pressure for rule-of-law improvements; Zapatista uprising in age of CNN — international attention changing calculus
unique_aspects: Longest-running competitive authoritarian system in library. No-re-election rule as unique stabilising mechanism preventing personality cult while maintaining party dominance. Gradual self-democratisation ending in 2000 — only case of peaceful voluntary power transfer from long-ruling authoritarian party.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; IFE/INE data; LAPOP historical; CIDE Mexico City

leader: Lee Kuan Yew → Goh → Lee Hsien Loong
econ_conditions: Entrepôt trade hub → manufacturing → financial centre transition; GDP per capita from $500 (1965) to $23,000 (2000); state-directed capitalism via GLC sovereign wealth model; housing ownership as social control and stability mechanism
social: Multiracial society managed through ethnic quota systems; Confucian values discourse legitimising soft authoritarianism; meritocracy ideology justifying PAP dominance as competence; chilling effect via defamation suits against opposition figures
institutional: Westminster system maintained but gerrymandered effectively; Internal Security Act allowing detention without trial; defamation law weaponised against opposition; GRC group representation constituencies reducing opposition viability
political: PAP never lost a general election; opposition allowed to win a few seats as safety valve; Goh Chok Tong managed succession without instability; Transparency International consistently high — corruption genuinely low
external: Cold War: US valued stable anti-communist Singapore; ASEAN founding member — regional legitimacy; small state logic: vulnerability used to justify internal discipline
unique_aspects: Only case where genuine competence and low corruption coexist with systematic political control. Lee Kuan Yew paradox: authoritarian by any institutional measure, yet delivering outcomes superior to most democracies. Defies standard backsliding narrative — no deterioration arc, just stable managed pluralism.
data_notes: V-Dem 1959–2024; Elections Department Singapore; IPS survey data; Straits Times archives

econ_conditions: Marshall Plan $1.4bn injection restarting industrial base; currency reform 1948 (Deutschmark) ending hyperinflation; Wirtschaftswunder — economic miracle legitimising new democracy; Codetermination model giving workers institutional voice
social: Denazification — partial and contested but establishing new norms; constitutional patriotism replacing ethnic nationalism; generational replacement of Nazi-era elites by 1960s; collective guilt processing — never complete but publicly institutionalised
institutional: Basic Law drafted to be collapse-resistant — no Article 48 equivalent; 5% threshold preventing small party fragmentation; constructive vote of no confidence preventing government collapse; Federal Constitutional Court with genuine independence from day one
political: CDU/SPD alternation establishing legitimate competition; Adenauer's Western integration strategy removing revisionist temptation; rearmament within NATO framework — sovereignty constrained but stable; Berlin question managed without escalation for 40 years
external: Allied occupation providing external enforcement of democratic norms; NATO membership removing security dilemma; European integration project giving Germany institutional home
unique_aspects: Only successful democracy-building on the ruins of a collapsed one within the same generation. Constitutional design specifically addressing Weimar failure points — Basic Law is essentially a list of lessons from 1933. External enforcement during consolidation phase proved essential.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Bundesarchiv Koblenz; Adenauer Foundation; Marshall Plan documentation

econ_conditions: Technocratic Opus Dei economic modernisation 1960s creating middle class; transition during oil shock — economic pressure during political change; Moncloa Pact 1977 — parties agreeing on economic rules first; tourism and emigrant remittances providing economic cushion
social: Generational change: post-civil war generation without direct trauma; regional nationalist movements (ETA, Catalan) as spoiler threat; Church stepping back from political role unlike 1930s; strong civil society emerged under late Francoism
institutional: Suárez reform from within — using Francoist institutions to dismantle Francoism; King Juan Carlos as legitimising bridge figure — surprising reformer; army officers who had served Franco accepting transition; 1977 Amnesty Law — no accountability for either side
political: Pacted transition — all sides accepting impunity for past; first democratic elections 1977 producing centrist result not polarisation; attempted coup 1981 (23-F) failing and actually strengthening democracy; PSOE socialist victory 1982 completing consolidation
external: European Community membership as carrot and anchor; NATO membership debate providing focus for democratic debate; Basque and Catalan pressure creating urgency for transition
unique_aspects: Modelo de transición — negotiated elite pact becoming the global template for democratic transitions. Amnesty Law: deliberately trading accountability for stability — ethical compromise that worked politically. King's role is unreplicable — hereditary monarch choosing democracy over the power he was given.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Fundación Transición Española; Congreso de los Diputados archives

econ_conditions: Chaebol-led export miracle creating educated middle class; GDP growth 9%+ annually through 1980s; worker organising challenging chaebol dominance; 1988 Olympics as international legitimacy moment
social: Gwangju massacre 1980 as founding trauma of democracy movement; student movement maintaining pressure throughout 1980s; Minjung movement combining labour and democracy activism; middle class joining student demands by 1987
institutional: Military as explicit political actor; Chun Doo-hwan regime attempting permanent institutionalisation; June 1987 declaration — military blinked under mass pressure; Roh Tae-woo transition figure with military credentials
political: Kim Dae-jung and Kim Young-sam opposition split repeatedly aiding regime; 1987 June Democracy Movement — mass protests forcing direct elections; first peaceful transfer to opposition party 1997; chaebol-political nexus creating ongoing corruption vulnerability
external: US pressure for political liberalisation increasing post-Cold War; Olympics hosting creating international visibility; North Korea threat paradoxically both enabling and limiting military role
unique_aspects: Economic development creating its own political transition pressure — middle class created by the authoritarian developmental state became the constituency that ended it. Gwangju massacre unlike anything in European transitions — state violence at this scale as democracy movement origin point.
data_notes: V-Dem 1948–2024; Korea Democracy Foundation; KSDC; Gwangju Uprising documentation

econ_conditions: Soviet-style economy failing — legitimacy crisis; debt to Western banks creating opening for Western leverage; shock therapy 1990 — radical but effective economic transition; unemployment spike from transition creating short-term social pain
social: Catholic Church as institutional backbone of civil society; Solidarity as cross-class coalition — workers + intellectuals unusual; martial law 1981 — crushing but not eliminating the movement; underground civil society (samizdat, flying universities) during martial law
institutional: Roundtable negotiations — regime negotiating its own managed exit; partially free elections June 1989 — Solidarity won everything it contested; Mazowiecki government accepting communist-era officers in security positions; lustration debate — accountability vs stability tension
political: Jaruzelski bargaining from weakness not strength in 1989; Gorbachev's signal that Soviet tanks wouldn't come this time; Solidarity umbrella fragmenting post-victory into competing parties; Wałęsa's difficult transition from union leader to president
external: Soviet Gorbachev factor — unique permissive external environment; Western economic support conditional on democratic progress; Pope John Paul II as symbolic anchor for Polish national identity
unique_aspects: Only case where a labour movement became the primary vehicle for democratic transition. Church-intelligentsia-worker coalition is unreplicable elsewhere. Roundtable model became an export — Hungary, Czechoslovakia followed within months. Underground infrastructure maintained during martial law proved decisive.
data_notes: V-Dem 1918–2024; IPN (Institute of National Remembrance); Solidarity archives Gdańsk; roundtable documentation

econ_conditions: Drought and oil shock creating economic pressure 1973–74; Indira Gandhi's populist garibi hatao — poverty elimination failing; railway workers strike 1974 — JP movement beginning; economic stress providing justification for emergency declaration
social: Allahabad High Court voiding Indira's election — legal trigger; JP Narayan movement crossing class and party lines; forced sterilisation programme alienating rural voters catastrophically; free press suspended but foreign press and BBC still accessible
institutional: Emergency powers in constitution used for first time; preventive detention of opposition leaders including JP Narayan; Supreme Court capitulated initially; Election Commission retained nominal independence
political: Indira declared emergency June 25 1975 citing external threats; Janata coalition assembling from disparate opposition; 1977 election called by Indira — unexpected loss; Janata government failing to consolidate — Indira returned 1980
external: Cold War context — US indifferent, Soviet support for Indira; Non-Aligned Movement providing international legitimacy cover; Bangladesh war victory 1971 had made Indira appear invincible
unique_aspects: Only case of democratic resilience via electoral self-correction — the person who imposed the emergency also called the election that ended it. Janata coalition's failure after victory shows fragility of negative coalitions. India's federal structure and free press (even suppressed) proved more resilient than expected.
data_notes: V-Dem 1947–2024; Election Commission of India; CSDS-Lokniti; Shah Commission report

econ_conditions: Postwar reconstruction via Marshall Plan; rapid modernisation (Trente Glorieuses beginning); colonial wars (Indochina, Algeria) consuming military budget; inflation and balance of payments as chronic instability
social: Communist party largest in France — Cold War complication; decolonisation pressure — settlers in Algeria as political veto player; Fourth Republic produced 21 governments in 12 years; de Gaulle waiting in Colombey-les-Deux-Églises as permanent alternative
institutional: Proportional representation producing ungovernable assemblies; president ceremonial — no executive authority; prime ministers falling on average every 6 months; constitutional reform blocked by parties benefiting from instability
political: Algerian crisis 1958 as forcing mechanism — army generals threatening coup; de Gaulle called in as only figure all sides could accept; Fifth Republic constitution drafted around de Gaulle's preferences; referendum legitimising new constitution with 80% approval
external: Algerian war creating military insubordination; NATO and Western integration requiring stable partner; Suez crisis 1956 humiliating France internationally
unique_aspects: Self-reform under threat rather than external imposition or collapse. Fourth Republic voted itself out of existence. Successor system (Fifth Republic) designed around one man — a constitutionally institutionalised elected monarchy that has outlasted de Gaulle by 60 years.
data_notes: V-Dem 1789–2024; Archives Nationales France; de Gaulle Foundation; IFOP historical surveys

econ_conditions: Post-war miracle: 10% growth 1955–1973; iron triangle: LDP-bureaucracy-business symbiosis; 1990 bubble collapse ending economic legitimacy; keiretsu cross-shareholding creating stability but inefficiency
social: 1955 System: conservative dominance accepted by exhausted society; zainichi Korean minority as second class; salaryman culture — corporate loyalty over political engagement; gradual ageing creating structural fiscal pressure
institutional: MITI bureaucracy as real government behind LDP facade; faction system within LDP providing internal pluralism; Article 9 pacifism constraining military ambitions; Supreme Court extremely deferential to government
political: JSP as permanent opposition never expected to govern; 1993 LDP split ending 38-year dominance — but LDP returned 1994; political money scandals recurring but not destabilising; consensus decision-making (nemawashi) slowing reform
external: US security umbrella removing defence burden; Cold War giving Japan clear strategic alignment; trade friction with US creating internal political pressure
unique_aspects: One-party democracy without alternation for 38 years via internal faction rotation as substitute for inter-party competition. LDP is itself a coalition — policy competition happens within the party. No other democracy has managed this length of single-party dominance without becoming authoritarian.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; National Diet Library Japan; Jiji Press historical archive

econ_conditions: Military regime leaving hyperinflation as parting gift; Plano Cruzado, Bresser, Verão — three failed stabilisation plans; Plano Real 1994 — finally working, legitimising democracy; debt crisis limiting government capacity during transition
social: Diretas Já movement — 1 million in streets demanding direct elections; landless movement and unions as left pressure on transition; evangelical church emerging as political force; Amazon frontier conflicts creating governance challenge
institutional: Abertura — gradual military opening not sudden transition; Tancredo Neves dying before inauguration — Sarney accident; 1988 Constitution — most rights-generous in world, fiscally unworkable; Collor impeachment 1992 — institutions working as designed
political: Military retaining amnesty and control of transition terms; party fragmentation — 30+ parties in Congress by 1990s; Fernando Collor — first direct election president, impeached for corruption; Lula losing three times before 1994 context ready for him
external: IMF conditionality shaping economic policy space; Washington Consensus as external economic pressure; drug trafficking beginning to create parallel governance in favelas
unique_aspects: Collor impeachment 1992 — first successful presidential impeachment in Latin American democratic history, and it worked. Demonstrated Brazilian institutions had genuine self-correcting capacity. Hyperinflation-to-stability transition most extreme in library: annual inflation 2,000%+ before Plano Real.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; TSE Brazil; IBGE; Plano Real documentation; Collor impeachment congressional records

econ_conditions: Communist economy stagnating — reformers proposing market elements; Prague Spring economic liberalisation alongside political opening; Ota Šik market socialist model threatening Soviet economic model; consumer goods shortages fuelling reform demand
social: Intellectual ferment — Literární noviny as reform voice; Slovak national aspirations complicating federation question; youth movement energised — generation without Stalin-era fear; writers union as civil society substitute
institutional: Dubček reforming from within Communist Party — not against it; Action Programme April 1968 — party-led liberalisation; censorship abolished but party structure maintained; Warsaw Pact treaty providing legal pretext for intervention
political: Reform from within Communist Party — no Western-style opposition; Dubček personally trusted by reformers and initially by Moscow; 20 days negotiation after invasion — Dubček capitulating under duress; normalisation 1969–1989 — 20 years of frozen society
external: Brezhnev Doctrine — socialist gains irreversible; Warsaw Pact invasion August 21 1968 — 500,000 troops; Western non-response — outside Soviet sphere of influence; 1956 Hungary precedent — world knew intervention was possible
unique_aspects: Pure external suppression — reform movement not defeated internally, militarily crushed. Socialism with a human face had broad popular support. Unlike Hungary 1956 there was no armed resistance — passive non-cooperation instead. 20-year normalisation that followed is the most complete freezing of a society in the library.
data_notes: V-Dem 1918–2024; ÚSD (Institute for Contemporary History Prague); Charter 77 documentation; Warsaw Pact invasion records

econ_conditions: Economy growing rapidly under junta — legitimacy through growth; tourism boom funding regime; Cyprus crisis creating economic disruption 1974; post-junta stabilisation requiring Marshall Plan equivalent
social: Conservative rural society vs modernising urban Athens; student protests 1973 — polytechnic uprising brutally crushed; diaspora Greek opposition internationally visible; Church ambiguous — neither clearly supporting nor opposing junta
institutional: King Constantine failed counter-coup December 1967 — legitimacy problem; constitution suspended parliament dissolved; military governing directly — no civilian facade maintained; torture documented by Council of Europe — early international rights monitoring
political: Coup justified as preventing communist electoral victory; Papadopoulos liberalisation attempt 1973 — regime fracturing; Ioannidis hardliner coup against Papadopoulos; Cyprus disaster 1974 — Makarios coup triggering Turkish invasion collapsing regime
external: US ambivalent — Cold War positioning over democratic norms; NATO membership maintained despite democratic backsliding; Cyprus crisis as external shock ending regime; Karamanlis return from Paris exile — transition managed by external figure
unique_aspects: Only case ended primarily by foreign policy disaster rather than internal pressure or external military force. Cyprus adventure was the regime's own choice — miscalculation producing the external shock destroying it. Clean transition to Karamanlis and subsequent EU membership makes it the fastest successful democratic recovery in the library.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Historical Archive of the Greek Parliament; Council of Europe torture documentation; Cyprus crisis records

econ_conditions: 1980s debt crisis and IMF austerity destroying federal economic bargain; hyperinflation 1989: 2,600% — economic legitimacy collapse; republic-level economic divergence: Slovenia 4x Serbia per capita; privatisation creating nationalist-connected oligarchs
social: 1974 constitution creating republic-level identities over Yugoslav; memory politics: WWII Ustaše-Chetnik crimes reactivated by elites; Kosovo 1989 — Milošević's speech at Gazimestan beginning ethnic mobilisation; refugee flows from wars creating further radicalisation
institutional: Collective presidency without Tito unable to resolve disputes; JNA (army) transforming from Yugoslav to Serbian instrument; republic-level institutions gaining legitimacy as federal lost it; international recognition of Slovenia and Croatia premature — accelerating war
political: Milošević instrumentalising Kosovo grievance for Serbian nationalism; Tuđman HDZ reviving Ustaše symbols — deliberate provocation; Izetbegović caught between Serb and Croat nationalist projects; Dayton 1995 freezing rather than resolving ethnic geography
external: German premature recognition of Slovenia/Croatia; UN arms embargo disadvantaging Bosnian government; NATO intervention 1999 in Kosovo — late but decisive; EU offering no membership anchor during critical transition years
unique_aspects: Only case of complete state dissolution via ethnic war in library. Unlike other cases there was no single regime to fall — multiple regimes fell simultaneously. International community failures as important as domestic variables. Dayton architecture created frozen conflicts rather than resolution.
data_notes: V-Dem 1918–2024; ICTY documentation; ICMP (missing persons); Dayton Agreement text; UNHCR displacement data

econ_conditions: Oil price collapse 1998 destroying Punto Fijo system legitimacy; Caracazo 1989 — IMF austerity riots killing 300 traumatising political class; Chávez using oil windfall for Misiones social programmes; PDVSA purge after 2002 strike — oil company as political instrument
social: Extreme inequality — Gini among highest in Latin America; Chávez as Bolívarian racial-class identity symbol for poor; middle class and business community as permanent opposition; barrios as political mobilisation base bypassing traditional structures
institutional: 1999 Constitution — Chávez rewrote rules via referendum; Supreme Court packed with chavistas after 2004; Electoral council (CNE) gradually losing independence; National Assembly bypassed by enabling laws giving decree power
political: Coup attempt 2002 — Chávez survived radicalising trajectory; oil strike 2002–03 — Chávez won purging PDVSA; 2004 recall referendum — Chávez won demoralising opposition; chavismo as movement not party — personalismo maximum
external: Cuba providing intelligence and security apparatus training; US coup support 2002 — backing anti-Chávez plotters; ALBA regional integration as counter to US influence; Colombia conflict spillover creating security justification
unique_aspects: Oil revenue as democracy-dissolving mechanism — the resource curse operating in real time. Misiones model of bypassing existing institutions with parallel social programmes is unique. 2002 coup attempt and its defeat was the turning point — Chávez drew the lesson that only complete institutional control would secure his position.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Carter Center 2004 recall data; PROVEA human rights; CNE official data

econ_conditions: 2008 IMF bailout legitimacy crisis inherited; EU structural funds captured as patronage (~6bn EUR/yr); NER oligarch network receiving state contracts; strategic sectors renationalised: energy, banking, media

institutional: 2/3 supermajority enabling constitutional rewrite without referendum; Constitutional Court packed and jurisdiction stripped; electoral law redrawn — gerrymandering + reduced districts; Media Council controlling broadcast licensing
political: Fidesz changing rules between each election cycle; opposition coordination failure across multiple cycles; 2022 united opposition still lost — system too tilted; EU Article 7 proceedings blocked by unanimity rule
external: EU membership as unique constraint floor; Brussels used as external scapegoat — mirrors Mussolini/Versailles; no bilateral military pressure
unique_aspects: EU paradox: membership simultaneously constrains and enables. Illiberal democracy framing — openly redefining democracy rather than pretending to uphold it. Social media enabling direct leader-to-voter communication bypassing captured traditional media. Fastest modern consolidation using legal templates pioneered by Mussolini.
data_notes: V-Dem 1900–2024; Freedom House; Media ownership registry; EU rule of law reports

institutional: 2016 coup attempt — purge of 150,000; 2017 presidential system referendum; HSYK judicial council restructured; bar associations attacked

İmamoğlu tension — system not fully closed unlike Hungary. NATO nuclear umbrella creates unique external constraint.

institutional: National Assembly bypassed via Supreme Court 2017; Constituent Assembly as parallel legislature; 2019 Guaidó parallel presidency; electoral council fully captured — no credible elections since 2013

econ_conditions: Lava Jato corruption scandal delegitimising PT; 2015–16 recession creating openness to outsider; Bolsonaro economic liberalism (Guedes) vs social conservatism — coalition tension; post-COVID commodity boom reducing economic urgency
social: Evangelical church as primary Bolsonaro institutional base; WhatsApp misinformation networks as alternative information ecosystem; gun ownership liberalisation; anti-PT sentiment stronger than pro-Bolsonaro
institutional: STF (Supreme Court) as main institutional resistance — Moraes taking aggressive counter-authoritarian stance; electoral system resilience — Bolsonaro attacked but couldn't break it; military ultimately refusing to support January 8 coup attempt
political: Bolsonaro signalling coup for 2 years — military and institutions prepared; Lula 50.9% vs 49.1% — no mandate, maximum polarisation; January 8 2023 — Capitol-style attack on institutional buildings; military inaction during January 8
external: US: Biden administration clear on election legitimacy; OAS: monitoring; International press: documenting coup signals; Lula: regional democratic solidarity
